clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by mutations in GJB6 (connexin 30); the classic triad is nail dystrophy, hypotrichosis and palmoplantar keratoderma.
The term hidrotic denotes preserved sweating: eccrine sweat glands and thermoregulation are normal, distinguishing it from the far commoner hypohidrotic (anhidrotic) ectodermal dysplasias.
Teeth are characteristically normal, another key contrast with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, which features hypodontia and conical teeth.
Nail changes are the most constant feature: nails are thick, slow-growing, discoloured, brittle or hypoplastic, and prone to recurrent paronychia and infection.
Hair is sparse, fine, brittle and slow-growing, with reduced eyebrows, eyelashes and body hair, and progressive scalp alopecia may occur.
Palmoplantar keratoderma with hyperpigmentation over the knuckles, elbows and knees is common, and digital clubbing may be seen.
Facies, sweating, intelligence and life expectancy are all normal.
Classically described in French-Canadian kindreds but reported worldwide.
reference.pathophysiology: Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (Clouston syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous missense mutations in GJB6 on chromosome 13q12, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin 30 (Cx30). Connexins oligomerise into connexons (hemichannels) that dock between adjacent cells to form intercellular gap junctions, permitting direct exchange of ions and small signalling molecules between epidermal, hair-follicle and nail-matrix keratinocytes. The GJB6 mutations are thought to act predominantly through a dominant mechanism, either gain-of-function or dominant-negative, producing abnormal channels or disrupting the trafficking and assembly of connexons, which impairs keratinocyte communication and thereby the proliferation and differentiation of ectodermal appendages. This disturbs nail-plate, hair-shaft and palmoplantar epidermal formation while sparing the eccrine sweat glands and the teeth, giving the characteristic hidrotic pattern. Because eccrine secretory function is intact, thermoregulation is preserved, in contrast to the EDA-, EDAR- and EDARADD-related hypohidrotic forms in which sweating is deficient.
additionalDifferentials: Hypohidrotic (anhidrotic) ectodermal dysplasia (EDA, EDAR, EDARADD): hypohidrosis, hypodontia and characteristic facies
Pachyonychia congenita (keratin genes KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT16, KRT17): hypertrophic nail dystrophy and palmoplantar keratoderma
Isolated or other inherited palmoplantar keratodermas
Nail-patella syndrome (LMX1B): nail dysplasia with skeletal anomalies
Dyskeratosis congenita: nail dystrophy with mucosal leukoplakia and bone-marrow failure
Other connexin disorders, such as GJB2/GJB6-related deafness with skin phenotypes including KID syndrome
Acquired causes of nail dystrophy and alopecia, such as chronic onychomycosis or lichen planus
additionalInvestigations: Detailed clinical assessment and family pedigree consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
Molecular genetic testing of GJB6 to confirm the diagnosis
Dermatoscopic and clinical examination of nails, hair and palmoplantar skin
Skin or nail biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain, to exclude mimics
Nail mycology to identify or treat secondary onychomycosis
Audiological assessment if features suggest an overlapping connexin phenotype
Trichoscopy or hair-shaft microscopy to characterise the hypotrichosis
redFlags: Recurrent or severe nail and periungual infections requiring treatment
New or atypical lesions arising within areas of keratoderma, warranting exclusion of malignancy
Hearing impairment suggesting an overlapping connexin-related syndrome
Rapidly progressive alopecia or features atypical for Clouston syndrome, prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is compatible with a normal lifespan and normal intelligence; morbidity is largely cosmetic and relates to nail, hair and palmoplantar problems and their secondary infections, which are managed symptomatically.
pitfalls: Confusing it with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia and wrongly expecting impaired sweating or dental anomalies.
Attributing the nail changes solely to onychomycosis and missing the underlying genetic disorder.
Overlooking the diagnosis when palmoplantar keratoderma dominates the clinical picture.
Failing to take a family history that would reveal the dominant inheritance pattern.
references: Reference reviews on the ectodermal dysplasias
Clinical genetics references on connexin disorders
management: Emollients and keratolytics (topical urea or salicylic acid, oral retinoids in severe cases) for palmoplantar keratoderma
Meticulous nail care with prompt antifungal and antibacterial treatment of onychomycosis and recurrent paronychia
Cosmetic measures such as wigs and hairpieces for hypotrichosis and progressive scalp alopecia
Regular dermatological review of nails, hair and palmoplantar skin
Genetic counselling regarding autosomal dominant GJB6 (connexin 30) inheritance, with family screening
Psychological support for the largely cosmetic morbidity
Audiological assessment where features suggest an overlapping connexin phenotype
